- Law No. 13/005 of 15 January 2013 on the status of military personnel of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo; - Law No. 13/013 of 01 June 2013 on the status of career personnel of the National Police; - Organic Law No. 13/026 of 15 October 2013 on the organisation and functioning of the Constitutional Court; - Law No. 13/011 of 21 March 2013 establishing the National Human Rights Commission. - Law No. 15/001 of 12 February 2015 amending and supplementing the law organising presidential, legislative, provincial, urban, municipal and local elections as amended by Law No. 11/003 of 25 June 2011. - Law No. 016/08 of 15 July 2016 amending and supplementing the Family Code of 1987.

The Commission takes note of the adoption of the following texts: i. The adoption of various legal texts on torture, namely: - Law No. 11/008 of 9 July 2011 criminalising torture; - Directive No. AG/0793/10 of 23 June 2010 of the Auditor General of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo on torture; - Instruction No. 0905 PNC/CIAT Général/084/SVJur&Cont. /2015 of 7 May 2015 on the humanisation of the services of the General Commissariat of the Congolese National Police; - Instruction by Letter No. 1981/PNC/CG/COMDT/2014 of 16 July 2014 from the Commissioner General of the Congolese National Police to all Unit Commanders and Pool Heads to ensure that they strictly respect the legality of acts in the judicial proceedings opened in the offices, in particular as regards torture; ii. The organisation by the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights of an education campaign for the security forces and the population on the Law of July 2011; iii. The monitoring of lock-ups and prisons by the Ministry of Human Rights; iv. The strengthening of the capacities of Judicial Police Officers on the rights of arrested persons, in collaboration with the United Nations Joint Human Rights Office; v. The organisation by the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights (July 2012-November 2013) of a national campaign to popularise Law No. 11/008 of 09 July 2011 criminalising torture for the defence and security forces and the heads of the prison services in 11 provincial capitals and cities, and of another for judicial personnel (Magistrates and Lawyers), prison administration personnel and certain civil society organisations, as well as several awareness-raising campaigns on the criminalisation of torture with the support of technical and financial partners, in particular the United Nations Joint Human Rights Office.

The Commission notes the following: i. The strengthening of the judicial apparatus through the recruitment of magistrates and the establishment of tribunaux de paix in all provinces to facilitate access to justice for litigants; ii. The 20% salary increase for all 3,750 civil and military magistrates with a view to strengthening their independence; iii. The implementation of the legal and judicial assistance programme, in collaboration with the various bar associations of the country; iv. The special protection provided to witnesses and victims of sexual violence; v. The strengthening of the capacities of the police services and judicial bodies, by undertaking the following actions: - Continued installation of specialised courts in 2013, in particular commercial, labour and children's courts; - Establishment of a judicial support unit within the military justice system, currently being piloted in the East; - Appointment by presidential orders of 01 June 2013 of Magistrates with a view to making operational the newly created tribunaux de paix, commercial courts, children's courts and labour courts. - Continuation of judicial system reform programmes with the adoption of new laws including: Organic Law No. 13/00-B of 11 April 2013 on the organisation, functioning and jurisdiction of the courts of the judicial order; Organic Law No. 13/010 of 19 February 2013 on procedure before the Court of Cassation and the law on the organisation and functioning of the Constitutional Court vi.

The organisation of regular training sessions for Magistrates and judicial auxiliaries by the Ministry of National Defence and Veterans and the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights, with the support of international and national partners (MONUSCO and others); vii. The adoption of Prime Ministerial Decree No. 11/01 of 5 January 2011 fixing the jurisdictions and ordinary seats of the Children's Courts in order to allow their establishment; viii. The adoption of Orders No. 001/CAB/MIN/J&DH/2011 and No. 002/CAB/J&DH/2011 respectively establishing secondary seats of the Children's Courts and fixing their jurisdictions, and grouping the jurisdictions of the Children's Courts for the execution of custody, education and preservation measures, and Judicial Organisation Order No. 029/CAB/MIN/J&DH/2013 of 28 January 2013 on the Establishment, Organisation and Functioning of Local Committees for the Supervision of the Management of the Budget of Provincial Central Prisons and Detention Camps; ix.

The construction and rehabilitation of some twenty buildings housing the Courts and Tribunals, as well as the Offices of the special units of the national police responsible for combating sexual violence in the cities of Goma, Bukavu, Kindu, Bandundu and Bunia.

The Commission commends the Congolese State for putting in place numerous measures to improve conditions of detention through: i. The adoption by the Minister of Justice and Human Rights of Judicial Organisation Order No. 029/CAB/MIN/J&DH/2013 of 28 January 2013 on the establishment, organisation and functioning of the local committees for the supervision of the management of the budget of Provincial Central Prisons and Detention Camps, which introduces important innovations in the management of penitentiary establishments and establishes, for each Prison, a Committee for the management of the funds allocated to feeding prisoners; the regular inspection of lock-ups and other places of detention by public prosecutors; the monitoring of places of detention by the Protection Directorate of the General Secretariat for Human Rights; the strengthening of the capacities of judicial police officers on the rights of arrested persons; ii. The assignment to the CNDH of the responsibility to visit places of detention periodically throughout the Republic.

The Commission takes note of the existence of: i. the bill on the decriminalisation of press offences in favour of media professionals submitted to Parliament; ii. The adoption of Edict No. 001/2016 of 10 February 2016 on the protection of human rights defenders and journalists in South Kivu Province. iii. The bill on access to information submitted to Parliament; iv. The establishment of the Higher Council for Broadcasting and Communication (CSAC) by Organic Law No. 11/001 of 10 January 2011;
The Commission commends the State for its efforts to safeguard the right to life, in particular by observing a moratorium on the death penalty since 2003.

The Commission takes note of the following: i. The adoption of Ministerial Order No. 219/CAB/MINJ&DH/2011 of 13 June 2011 on the establishment, organisation and functioning of a Human Rights Defenders Protection Unit; ii. The efforts undertaken to finalise the law on the protection of defenders, currently under way, in conformity with the recommendations of the African Commission and in accordance with the provisions of the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Defenders.

The Commission takes note of the Government's initiation of a policy of major public works, the implementation of which has led to the creation of new jobs for the national workforce (156,887 jobs created from 2011 to 2013).

The Commission notes with appreciation the following: i. The adoption in March 2010 of a new education policy (Strategy for the development of primary, secondary and vocational education 2010-2016) with three major objectives: - to increase access, accessibility, equity and retention at the different levels of education and in particular in basic education; - to improve the quality and relevance of education and; - to strengthen the governance of the sector; ii. The progressive provision of free primary, secondary and vocational education, with the development of a national Education strategy launched in 2010 and the implementation of the interim education plan (2012-2014); iii. The improvement of access to education in accordance with the Interim Education Plan (PIE); iv. The construction of schools and health centres; v. The increase in the gross enrolment rate from 83.4% to 98% between 2007 and 2012, thanks to free education; vi. The construction and rehabilitation of school infrastructure (1,000 schools, of which 128 have already been built, 513 are under construction and 149 schools through the basic education support project "PROSEB"); vii. The construction of training and resource centres for the continuing training of teachers (Kinshasa, Bandundu, Kalemie, Kolwezi, Kikwit, Mbandaka, Kisangani), viii. The increase in the share of the national budget devoted to education, from 15% to 17% (2014); ix. The provision of textbooks for primary school pupils and of the teaching guide for teachers; x. The adoption of a human rights curriculum at the Faculty of Law of the University of Kinshasa by the Board of Directors of the Universities of the Congo, the body competent for drawing up programmes in the Universities.

The Commission welcomes the following: i. The taking into account of traditional medicine within the framework of the national health policy; ii. The facilitation of access to health care for the Congolese population, through the following measures: - Equipping and rehabilitation of 66 general referral hospitals and 330 health centres with the support of UNICEF and GAVI; - Rehabilitation of 120 other general referral hospitals and 1,280 health centres with the support of the Global Fund; - Rehabilitation of the Kinshasa Medical Education Institute. iii. The conduct of the following actions by the Government: - Distribution of impregnated mosquito nets for the prevention and management of malaria; - Vitamin A vaccination; - Establishment of the minimum conditions for emergency surgery and emergency obstetric care; - Vaccination campaigns against tuberculosis, poliomyelitis and yellow fever. iv. Increase in the life expectancy of men from 48 years (2011) to 53 years (2012) and that of women from 48 years (2011) to 56 years (2012)

The Commission notes with appreciation the following: i. The ongoing revision of the Land Law as part of the land reform, with a view to strengthening Articles 101 to 103 on expropriation for reasons of public utility in order to clearly redefine the appropriate mechanisms regarding the compensation of concession holders, ii. The preparation of a land-use planning scheme which will be accompanied by a land allocation plan according to rights holders but also according to uses, in order to put an end to the multiple land conflicts in the DRC and to the duality between written law and customary law.

The Commission notes with appreciation the following: i. The adoption and effective implementation of Law No. 8/0011 of 14 July 2008 on the protection of the rights of persons living with HIV/AIDS through the adoption of the following measures: - Presidential Order No. 11/023 of 18 March 2011 amending and supplementing Presidential Decree No. 04/029 of 17 March 2004 establishing and organising the PNMLS guides the national policy to combat HIV/AIDS and organises the structures for implementing the PSN at both central and decentralised levels; - Development of the National Strategic Plan 201-2013, 2014-2017; - Appointment of a Country Focal Point for Justice and Human Rights (Ministry of Justice); - Establishment of the "Rights and HIV" Group bringing together all the actors working in the field of human rights in connection with HIV; - Production of several documents (Review of the legal framework, Mapping of stakeholders and interventions, Report of the INDEX STIGMA Survey, Intervention strategy in prison settings, ...); - Organisation of several capacity-building sessions on Human Rights and HIV/AIDS; ii.

Establishment of the National AIDS Control Programme (PNLS) to halt and reverse the spread of HIV/AIDS, which coordinates all actions to combat HIV/AIDS, raises awareness among the population and ensures the care of AIDS patients and orphans; iii. Adoption of the National Strategic Plan 2018-2021, which aims, among other things, at promoting an environment conducive to the response to HIV/AIDS, free of all stigmatisation and discrimination against persons living with HIV/AIDS, affected persons, key populations and victims of sexual violence. iv.

The organisation of mass campaigns and the provision of medical kits for persons living with HIV/AIDS v. Strengthening of the adolescent health programme, created in 2003, whose mission is to raise awareness among adolescents, in school settings in particular and among young people in general, against early and unprotected sexual intercourse, early and unwanted pregnancies and the risks of contracting HIV/AIDS and sexually transmitted infections, as well as against unsafe abortions; vi. Establishment of centres for adolescents and young people throughout the country to offer specific reproductive health services, promote the use of condoms for the prevention of STIs and HIV/AIDS, and the creation of the Youth Network for the fight against HIV/AIDS;

The Commission notes the efforts made by the Congolese Government in favour of the promotion of indigenous populations, in particular through: i. The creation of a specific Ministry in charge of Customary Affairs. ; ii. The implementation of the recommendation of the Commission through the adoption of Ministerial Order No. 006 CAB/MIN/AFF-COUT/GM/AS/nmr/217 of 10 July 2017 on the establishment, organisation and functioning of consultative commissions for the settlement of customary disputes, in which customary dignitaries and chiefs of the indigenous Pygmy peoples are co-opted throughout the national territory; iii. Consultation of the populations in decision-making on the implementation of projects that concern them; iv. The consultation of indigenous populations on matters of expropriation, spoliation and eviction from their ancestral lands within the framework of the land reform.

The Commission notes with appreciation the following: i. The ratification, by Law No. 14/025 of 8 July 2014, of the African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa, adopted on 22 October 2009 in Kampala; ii. The existence of a draft law on the assistance and protection of internally displaced persons, prepared by an ad hoc commission of the Ministry of the Interior and Security; iii. The national integration options offered to Angolan and Rwandan refugees in the cessation clauses of their refugee status, which has been signed, in particular: - The granting of a temporary residence card serving as a residence permit in the DRC to former Angolan refugees who had requested local integration, pending the obtaining of passports from the Government of the Republic of Angola, which benefited 18,500 persons; - The exemption from the cessation clause for refugees who presented a genuine need for protection arising from previous persecution, thanks to which 631 persons were able to keep their refugee status.

The Commission notes with appreciation the following: i. The promulgation of the following laws: - Law No. 11/09 of 09 July 2011 on the fundamental principles relating to the protection of the environment; - Law No. 014/003 of 11 February 2014 on nature conservation. - Law No. 18/001 of 09 March 2018 amending and supplementing Law No. 007/2002 of 11 July 2002 on the Mining Code, which improves the existing legal framework on extractive industries through: ▪ The inclusion of the storage, holding and transport of mineral substances within the scope of this code; ▪ The restriction of eligibility for mining rights to legal entities only; ▪ The adoption of incentive measures for provinces with infrastructure deficits in order to enable their economic development; ▪ The taking into account of the principles and criteria of the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative; ▪ The clarification of the legal framework that may exceptionally authorise the export of minerals in the raw state; ▪ The replacement of the environmental opinion by the environmental certificate; ▪ The obligation to build the building housing the head office in the capital of the province of operation; ▪ The application of the rules of straight-line depreciation of fixed assets; ▪ The setting of the amount of share capital at no less than 40 percent of the resources necessary for the completion of the investment. ▪ The implementation of a mechanism for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation (REDD). ▪ Subscription, in 2012, to the three objectives of the "Sustainable Energy for All" initiative to be achieved by 2030:

(i) universal access to electricity, (ii) doubling the share of renewable energy in the energy mix to reach a ratio of at least 30% of the energy used in the country, and (iii) doubling energy efficiency. ii. The improvement of the governance of the sector and the launch of major hydroelectric projects; iii. The liberalisation of the electricity sector in all its branches (production, transmission and distribution) by a Law of June 2014; iv. Accession to various certification systems in order to prevent blood minerals from being placed on the market, such as: - The ICGLR regional certification mechanism (3T Coltan, Cassiterite, Wolframite and Gold); - The Kimberley Process, KP; - The OECD due diligence guidance for mining companies; - Interministerial Order No. 206/CAB/MIN/FINANCES/2010 of 15 October 2010 on the manual of procedures for the traceability of mining products from extraction to export.

The Commission takes note of the following: i. The existence of the directorate for the coordination of rehabilitation activities for persons with disabilities (DICOREPHA) within the Ministry of Social Affairs, which supervises the specialised services of the Ministry and civil society structures; ii. The existence of a Bill on the protection of persons with disabilities before Parliament (2015).
Limited financial resources for the effective implementation of State programmes, for the realisation of a number of rights, and for human rights institutions and organisations;
The recurrence of armed conflicts in the North-East of the country, which requires the allocation of a large part of the available resources to the imperative of pacifying the national territory;
Low awareness among the population of their rights;
The weight of sociological and cultural factors, the persistence of custom, and deeply rooted prejudices, in particular towards women, remain obstacles to the full realisation of women's rights.

Although the Commission positively appreciates the responses of the Democratic Republic of the Congo regarding the various recommendations relating to its combined periodic reports (8th, 9th and 10th) of 2010, it nevertheless notes that the report does not provide precise and detailed answers to certain concerns it raised during its dialogue with the Congolese Delegation.

The Commission notes: i. the non-ratification of the following human rights instruments - African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child - African Youth Charter; - African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance; - Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights - Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Older Persons. - The declaration under Article 34(6) of the Protocol establishing the Court; ii. The slowness of the process of ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty, and of abolishing the death penalty in the texts in force, in particular the Penal Code; iii. The slowness in depositing the instruments of ratification of the Kampala Convention, although it is indicated in the responses provided that the DRC ratified, by Law No. 14/025 of 8 July 2014, the African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa (Kampala Convention).
The Commission regrets the absence of information concerning the participation and representation of youth in the conduct of the country's public affairs.

The Commission notes the slowness of the process of ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty, and of abolishing the death penalty in the texts in force, in particular the Penal Code.
The Commission remains concerned about attacks and other human rights violations against persons on the basis of their real or perceived sexual identity or orientation.

The Commission remains concerned about: i. The low number of women magistrates in the judicial system as a whole, ii. The absence of women Chief Divisional Commissioners, Principal Commissioners and Divisional Commissioners, and the low representation of women Deputy Divisional Commissioners and Commissioners; iii. The absence of alternatives to imprisonment; iv. The persistence of lengthy pre-trial detention.

The Commission is concerned about the following: i. The dilapidated state of prisons; ii. The absence of disaggregated statistics on the number of detainees: women, men, minors, and foreign detainees as well as pregnant women; iii. The absence of figures on the percentage of prisoners in pre-trial detention iv. The lack of information on the treatment of vulnerable groups in prisons, in particular persons with disabilities v. The absence of information concerning health care and medical assistance; vi. The impossibility for civil society organisations to visit prisons and other detention centres, vii. Despite the reference to Children's Courts, there is no information on the number and care of children in conflict with the law; viii. The lack of popularisation of the Luanda Guidelines, ix. The number of prisons and prison officers x. The absence of a mechanism for the oversight of prisons by NGOs
The Commission notes the absence of a national law on access to information and the restrictions on citizens' access to the internet for security reasons.

The Commission finds the following: i. The insufficient capacity building of human rights defenders; ii. The slowness in the process of drafting and adopting a law on the protection of human rights defenders in accordance with international standards; iii. The lack of response by the State to the urgent appeals sent to it.
The need to speed up the land reform process, particularly the reform of the Land Law, and the effective implementation of the planned land-use plans.

The Commission regrets the low percentage of the budget devoted to health (8%), which does not comply with the requirement of the Abuja Declaration that States should devote at least 15% of their budget to health.
The Commission is concerned about the persistence of child labour, particularly in Coltan mines, despite the laws in force prohibiting this practice.

The Commission notes the absence of information concerning: i. The absence of information on the existence of a nutrition programme in addition to an ARV distribution programme to support persons living with HIV; ii. The slowness in amending Articles 37 and 39 of the law on the protection of PLHIV and affected persons, concerning the obligation for minors to be tested only with the permission and in the presence of their parents or guardians and the obligation to hand over HIV test results only to parents or guardians.
The Commission remains concerned about the slowness noted in the adoption by Parliament of the bill on the protection of the rights of indigenous peoples, pending since 2015;

The Commission notes the lack of information concerning: i. The number of companies engaged in extractive industries and their areas of activity; ii. The limitation of marginalised populations' access to electricity due to the liberalisation of the energy sector; iii. The level of artisanal mining in the country and the existence or not of programmes or policies aimed at monitoring or regulating this practice; iv. Government policy aimed at raising awareness of safety standards, in view of the threats to the environment and to the health of artisanal miners; v. The measures provided for in cases of violations of environmental standards or in cases where the activities of extractive industries lead to environmental degradation; vi. The lack of information on the remedy mechanism in cases of violations relating to extractive industries
The Commission remains concerned about the slowness in the adoption of the Bill on the protection of persons with disabilities, which has been before Parliament since 2015.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo should continue to comply with its obligations under Article 62 of the African Charter by implementing its recommendations;

The Democratic Republic of the Congo should: i. Take all necessary measures to speed up the process of ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty, and abolish the death penalty in the texts in force, in particular the Penal Code. ii. Take steps to ratify the following human rights instruments: - African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child - African Youth Charter; - African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance; - Protocol on the Statute of the African Court of Justice and Human Rights - Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Older Persons. - Deposit the instruments of ratification of the Kampala Convention - Make the declaration under Article 34(6) of the Maputo Protocol.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo should take into account the youth dimension in the implementation of the right to take part in the conduct of the public affairs of the country.

The State should take the necessary measures to: i. Speed up the process of ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty; ii. Abolish the death penalty in the texts in force, in particular the Penal Code.
The State should ensure that no person is a victim of attacks and other human rights violations on the basis of their real or perceived sexual identity or orientation.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo should: i. Take the necessary measures to increase the number of women in the judicial system; ii. Put in place policies for the effective presence of women in decision-making positions within the Police; iii. Provide for alternatives to imprisonment; iv. Take the necessary measures to put an end to lengthy pre-trial detention.

The State should: i. Have disaggregated statistics on the number of detainees: women, men and minors, and the percentage of prisoners in pre-trial detention; ii. Ensure the proper treatment of vulnerable groups in prisons, in particular persons with disabilities; iii. Ensure that prisons have good medical equipment and that prisoners receive good medical care; iv. Adopt legislative measures that guarantee access for institutions and civil society organisations to visit prisons and other detention centres in the DRC in accordance with international standards; v. Make use of the Luanda Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-Trial Detention in Africa, while conducting training of police officers and reviewing laws and policies relating to arrest, police custody and pre-trial detention. vi. Set up an independent police oversight institution where civilians can freely report cases of human rights violations committed by the police.

The State should adopt a Law on access to information following the model of the Model Law on Access to Information for Africa developed and adopted by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights and ensure that access to the internet is free and open to citizens

The Commission recommends that the State: i. Continue and increase support and training activities with a view to strengthening the capacities of human rights defenders, so that they are better equipped; ii. Speed up the process of finalising the Bill for the protection of human rights defenders; iii. Follow up on the urgent appeals addressed to it.

The State should: i. Provide the number of companies engaged in extractive industries and their areas of activity; ii. Ensure that vulnerable populations can have access thereto through measures put in place for that purpose. iii. Monitor and support artisanal mining in the country through programmes or policies aimed at monitoring or regulating this practice; iv. Put in place a government policy aimed at raising awareness of safety standards, in view of the threats to the environment and to the health of artisanal miners; v. Provide for measures in cases of violations of environmental standards or in cases where the activities of extractive industries lead to environmental degradation.

The State must speed up the land reform process, particularly the reform of the Land Law, and the effective implementation of the planned land-use plans, while ensuring that it secures the rights of local communities and indigenous populations.

The State should take all appropriate measures to ensure that the laws adopted to prohibit child labour, particularly in Coltan mines, are strictly applied and that offenders are punished in accordance with the law, in order to effectively put an end to child labour.
The DRC should take the necessary measures to comply with the requirements of the Abuja Declaration, which require that at least 15% of the national budget be devoted to health.

The State, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, should: iii. Put in place a nutrition programme to complement the ARV distribution programme in order to support persons living with HIV; iv. Speed up the amendment of Articles 37 and 39 of the law on the protection of PLHIV and affected persons, concerning the obligation for minors to be tested only with the permission and in the presence of their parents or guardian and the obligation to hand over HIV test results only to parents or guardian.

The State should: - Speed up the process of adoption of the bill on the protection of the rights of indigenous populations before Parliament, pending since 2015; - Strengthen the participation of the populations in decision-making through the establishment of consultation mechanisms on projects that have an impact on their way of life; - Conduct awareness-raising campaigns among the populations with a view to reducing land conflicts.

The Commission encourages the State to speed up the process of adoption of the Bill on the protection of persons with disabilities, which has been before Parliament since 2015, and to ratify the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa, open for ratification since January 2018.
The Commission notes several positive aspects regarding the compliance by the Democratic Republic of the Congo with its obligations under the Maputo Protocol:

The Commission positively appreciates the submission of the first report in accordance with the provisions of Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol. This report is presented in two parts, one of which concerns the implementation of the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission notes with satisfaction the establishment of a legal framework for the protection of women's rights through the adoption of the following legislative texts and orders: - Law No. 06/018 of 20 July 2006 on the Congolese Penal Code, amending and supplementing the Decree of 30 January 1940 - Law No. 06/019 of 20 July 2006 on the Congolese Code of Criminal Procedure, amending and supplementing the Decree of 6 August 1959 - Law No. 73-021 of 20 July 1973 on the general property regime, the land and real estate regime and the security regime, as amended and supplemented to date - Law No. 001/2001 of 17 May 2001 on the organisation and functioning of political parties. - Law No. 08/005 of 10 June 2008 on public funding of political parties. - Law No. 08/011 of 14 July 2008 on the protection of the rights of persons living with HIV/AIDS and affected persons. - Law No. 09/001 of 10 January 2009 on child protection. - Law No. 15/013 of 1 August 2015 on the modalities of application of women's rights and parity. - Law No. 015/016 of 15 July 2016 amending and supplementing Law No. 87-010 of 1 August 1987 on the Family Code. - Edict No. 29/K.OCC/2015 of 18/05/2015 prohibiting degrading customs towards women in the province of Kasaï-Occidental - Edict No. 27/K.OCC/2015 of 18/05/2015 prohibiting the hiring and exploitation of children in mining areas in Kasaï-Occidental - Edict No. 001/bdd/2013 of 18/01/2013 on child protection in the province of Bandundu - National Programme for the Promotion of Women (2002) - Gender Mainstreaming Strategy (2004) - National Gender Policy (2009) - National Strategy to Combat Gender-Based Violence (2009) - National Strategy to Combat Infant and Maternal Morbidity and Mortality (2010) - National Strategy for the Integration of Gender in National Development Policies and Programmes (updated version of the 2004 strategy) - Priority Action Programme (PAP) (2012), governmental and sectoral - Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) (2016) - Government Priority Action Programme on Gender (2012) - Government Action Programme May 2012 - Roadmap for the implementation of women's rights (2012) - Government action plan for the implementation of Resolution 1325 (2013) - National Strategy for Gender-Sensitive Planning and Budgeting (2013) - Strategy for the Political Participation of Congolese Women in Democratic Governance (2015)

The Commission notes with appreciation the establishment of the following institutions: - The Ministry of Women, Family and Children and its specialised structures, in particular: ▪ The Unit for Studies and Planning for the Promotion of Women, the Family and Child Protection, abbreviated "CEPFE", created in 2007; ▪ The National Agency to Combat Violence against Women, Young Girls and Girls, abbreviated "AVIFEM", created in 2009; ▪ The National Fund for the Promotion of Women and the Protection of Children, abbreviated "FONAFEN", created in 2009; ▪ The Regional Centre for Research and Documentation on Women, Gender and Peacebuilding in the Great Lakes Region, abbreviated "CERED-GL", created in 2008; ▪ The National Centre for Documentation and Information on the Family, associated with CERED-GL, abbreviated "CENADIF/CNACR", created in 2008. - The National Council of Women and its provincial representations. - The Ministry of Justice and Human Rights. - The provincial Governments and provincial synergies - The National Human Rights Commission (CNDH); - The Inter-Ministerial Technical Committee for the preparation and follow-up of initial and periodic human rights reports; - The Parliamentary Networks on Human Rights and Gender.

The Commission notes: - The inclusion of the principle of equality between men and women in the Constitution of the country, applicable in all areas of national, economic, political, social and cultural life. - The prohibition by Article 13 of the Constitution of 18 February 2006 of any discriminatory measure in matters of education and access to public office or in any other matter; - The repeal of Article 3 of the former code of 1963, which required marital authorisation for a married woman to validly engage her services, by Law No. 015/2002 of 16 October 2002; - The adoption of various laws to prevent discrimination, in particular: ▪ The framework law on primary, secondary and vocational education as well as on higher and university education, which reaffirms the principle of equality and non-discrimination. Access to educational institutions at all levels, to fields or programmes of study, and to scholarships is guaranteed to all, without discrimination based on sex or of any other kind; ▪ Law No. 18/003 of 17 July 1981 on the status of career personnel of the public services of the State, which provides in its Article 8 for equal conditions of access to the public service for men and women; ▪ Law No. 06/006 of 9 March 2006 on the organisation of presidential, legislative, provincial, urban, municipal and local elections, which provides in its Article 4 that all Congolese of either sex have the right to participate in voting; ▪ Law No. 15/013 of 1 August 2015 on the modalities of application of women's rights and parity.

The Commission notes with appreciation the following: i. The criminalisation of rape and all forms of sexual violence in the Penal Code; ii. The adoption of Law No. 06/018 on the repression of sexual violence, which condemns the deliberate transmission of incurable sexually transmitted infections; iii. The establishment of legal clinics for the judicial support of victims of sexual violence; iv. The establishment in 2013 of the Office of the Special Adviser to the Head of State on combating sexual violence and the recruitment of children into armed groups; v.

Development of a National Strategy to Combat Gender-Based Violence to contribute to the prevention and reduction of sexual and gender-based violence, to the improvement of the holistic care of survivors of violence and to the rehabilitation of perpetrators of such acts, a strategy, coupled with an action plan, which defines government policy and the actions to be undertaken to combat this scourge, in particular: - The fight against impunity, protection and prevention, security sector reform, multi-sectoral assistance, and data and mapping; - Creation of a National Agency to Combat Violence against Women (AVIFEM); - Creation of a National Fund for the Promotion of Women and the Protection of Children (FONAFEN) - Establishment of the Unit for Studies and Planning for the Promotion of Women, the Family and Child Protection (CEPFE), the strategic structure of the Ministry in charge of gender issues, whose missions include collecting, processing and publishing statistical data on violence against women and children; - Creation of several sectoral thematic groups, as spaces for dialogue, including the Gender Thematic Group (GTG), one of whose sub-groups is devoted to sexual and gender-based violence in order to monitor the implementation of sectoral policies within the framework of the Growth and Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (DSCRP II). vi.

Organisation of several awareness-raising and education activities for the population, in particular the "Break the Silence" Campaign to combat sexual violence, conducted by the Office of the Special Adviser to the Head of State on combating sexual violence and the recruitment of children into armed groups; vii. The deployment, from 05 to 24 January 2013 in North and South Kivu, by the army's Civic, Patriotic Education and Social Action Service, of awareness-raisers to the units engaged in operations against the M23 on the rules of humanitarian law, particularly on sexual violence; viii.

Conviction by the Military Justice system of more than 150 perpetrators of rape, including a Brigadier General of the armed forces and a Senior Principal Commissioner of the Congolese National Police, the latter with definitive dismissal; ix. The development of key messages on United Nations Security Council Resolutions 1325, 1820, 1888, 1889 and their popularisation within FARDC Units; x. The integration of human rights notions into the FARDC training manuals; xi. The publication of a directive by the Prosecutor General of the Republic instructing Magistrates to deal promptly with all cases of sexual violence and not to grant provisional release to alleged perpetrators in detention; xii.

The establishment of units to combat sexual violence in all the Prosecutor's Offices of the Tribunaux de Grande Instance of the DRC; xiii. The organisation of vocational training for women victims of sexual violence and demobilised children, in particular in Nyiragongo in North Kivu province by the National Institute for Vocational Preparation (INPP).

The Commission commends the DRC for the following: i. The putting in place of measures to combat stereotypes, in particular: - The promotion of gender equality in the field of education, - The revision of the Family Code (development of the new gender-sensitive Family Code), - The adoption and promulgation of laws guaranteeing equal access to employment and social protection, - The ratification of the OHADA accounting plan, which places particular emphasis on non-discrimination between men and women in the economic field, - The encouragement and strengthening of the representation of women in political structures, etc... ii. The adoption of a National Strategy to Combat Gender-Based Violence, whose objectives are: - The fight against all forms of impunity in matters of sexual and gender-based violence, - Prevention and Protection through the empowerment of the rights of women and children, - Taking into account the sex-specific needs of women, - A multi-sectoral response to the needs of survivors of SGBV; - Regular management and monitoring of the information in the Database on the subject. iii. The conduct of various studies with a view to identifying the root causes of violence against women, measuring its consequences and taking adequate measures for its prevention and elimination, in particular: - Studies on the determinants of gender-based violence in conflict and non-conflict areas; - Provincial gender profiles; - The communication strategy for behaviour change in the fight against sexual and gender-based violence; - The study on the contradictory relationship between idealised hegemonic masculinity and the realities of men's lives; - The study on masculinity and the one on the transformation of masculinity; - The study on assistance to victims of sexual violence in the DRC; - Mapping of gender-based violence with a view to determining the types of violence to which women are exposed, their causes and consequences, and according to the involvement of socio-cultural factors linked to the different provinces of the country:

The Commission takes note of the legislative reforms undertaken by the State to address this situation: i. the two laws of 20 July 2006 on sexual violence provide for sanctions against perpetrators of harmful practices such as sexual mutilation, incitement of minors to debauchery, procuring, forced prostitution, sexual harassment and slavery, forced marriage, bestiality, deliberate transmission of sexually transmitted infections, trafficking and exploitation of children for sexual purposes, forced pregnancy and sterilisation, and prostitution and pornography involving children. ii. Article 407 of the Family Code set the age of marriage at 18 years.

The Commission takes note of the legal provisions aimed at combating sexual harassment, in particular: i. Articles 73 and 74 of the Labour Code, which provide for the termination of the contract by the employer or the worker if either commits serious misconduct. ii. The laws on sexual violence of 2006 punish sexual harassment under the offences provided for in the new Penal Code.

The Commission notes with satisfaction the following legislative measures adopted by the State: - The law on political parties, which prohibits discrimination based on ethnicity, religion, sex and language in the creation, organisation and functioning of political parties; - The organic law on the functioning of the Independent National Electoral Commission, which provides in its Article 7 that the appointment of members must take into account national representation, including that of women; - Law No. 11/013 of 11 August 2011 on the organisation and functioning of the Congolese National Police (PNC), which encourages and promotes the recruitment of women into the police through Articles 56 and 59 - Law No. 015/013 of 1 August 2015 on the modalities of application of women's rights and parity, which sets out the modalities for the application of these rights in accordance with Article 14 of the Constitution.

The Commission notes the inclusion of women in the process of peace prevention and maintenance (Article 10(1)) and in all aspects of post-conflict reconstruction and rehabilitation (Article 10(2)(e)) through the following actions: - Numerous commitments made at local, regional and international levels to restore peace and stability in the formerly conflict-affected areas and the initiation of several reforms to consolidate peace and security, and to ensure the reconstruction of the country; - Organisation each year of various information and education activities for women by women, by the Ministry of Women, Family and Children and by civil society organisations; - Organisation of reflection days by women from different sectors during the month of March of each year dedicated to women.

The Commission notes the targeted measures taken by the State, in particular: i. The elimination of obstacles that hinder girls' and boys' access to school, ii. The strengthening of the presence and retention of girls and women in higher education (science, mathematics and technology), iii. The reduction of the gap between men and women in basic functional literacy; iv. The elimination of obstacles that hinder the schooling of pregnant adolescent girls, v. The establishment of various programmes relating respectively to: • The acceleration of girls' schooling initiated by the State with the support of UNICEF; • The eradication of illiteracy; • The policy on opportunity costs specific to girls, with the aim of promoting the retention in primary school of vulnerable girls aged 12 and over, and; • The communication and mobilisation programme aimed at ensuring school mobilisation of girls. vi. The organisation of awareness-raising campaigns by the government in partnership with civil society organisations and technical and financial partners with flagship themes such as: "Girls and boys in school", "Education is a right for the child".

The Commission commends the State for the following: i. The creation, since 2003, of the National Adolescent Health Programme and the adoption of Ministerial Order No. 1250/CAB/MINIS/001 of 13 January 2003, which establishes a programme in charge of adolescent health whose mission is to protect adolescents against early and unprotected sexual intercourse, early and unwanted pregnancies and the risks of contracting HIV/AIDS and sexually transmitted infections, as well as against unsafe abortions, in school settings in particular and among young people in general; ii. The establishment of centres for adolescents and young people throughout the country to offer specific reproductive health services, promote the use of condoms for the prevention of STIs and HIV/AIDS, and the creation of the Youth Network for the fight against HIV/AIDS; iii. The integration, since 2014, into the formal education system of subjects relating to family and sexual life in order to combat the transmission of HIV/AIDS and sexually transmitted infections in school settings.

The Commission commends the State for the following: i. The adoption of appropriate legislative measures to ensure the protection of widows, in particular: - Article 16, paragraph 4 of the Constitution of 2006, which stipulates that no one may be subjected to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; - Law No. 87-010 of 1 August 1987 on the Family Code, which in its Articles 541 and 544 provides for the dissolution of marriage by operation of law upon the death of the husband and establishes sanctions against anyone who has imposed on the widower or widow or on their relatives degrading treatment or the performance of rites incompatible with human dignity. Articles 545, 758b, 760, 785 and 790 of the same law provide general information on the procedure for inheritance after the death of the spouse; - Law No. 13/013 of 1 June 2013 on the status of National Police personnel, in its Articles 246, 247, 248 and 249, determines the benefits and rights reserved for the spouse of a deceased police officer. The same applies to Law No. 13/005 of 15 January 2013 on the status of FARDC military personnel, in its Article 207; - The Decree-Law of 29 June 1961 on the organic framework of social security, in its Articles 41 and 43, grants a survivor's pension or allowance to the widow whose deceased spouse would have been entitled to a retirement pension; - Law No. 15/013 of 1 August 2015 on the modalities of application of women's rights and parity, in its Article 19, prohibits, in the event of death, the infliction of inhuman, humiliating and degrading treatment on the surviving spouse, on pain of judicial proceedings; ii. The repeal of the decree of 4 April 1950 relating to polygamy and the enshrinement of monogamy by the Family Code; iii. The organisation of a campaign for the regularisation of marriages before the civil status authorities with a view to improving widows' inheritance rights; iv. The removal of matters of the law of persons and of the family from the jurisdiction of customary courts in favour of the tribunaux de paix and the Tribunaux de Grande Instance; v. The regulation of succession by law vi. The adoption of the national social protection strategy and the awareness-raising and training of widows on empowerment.

The Commission notes the various actions taken by the State, such as: i. The putting in place of administrative measures such as Ministerial Order No. CAB/MIN/AFF.SO/053/95 of 25 March 1995 establishing the national directorate for the support of the elderly, whose mission is to oversee the functioning of hospices and homes for the housing and support of the elderly in geriatrics in the DRC; ii. The National Strategy for the social protection of vulnerable groups and the national fund for promotion and social service.

The Commission notes the existence of the directorate for the coordination of rehabilitation activities for persons with disabilities (DICOREPHA) within the Ministry of Social Affairs, which supervises the specialised services of the Ministry and civil society structures.

The Commission notes the establishment of a rural development fund to facilitate access to credit in rural areas. A microcredit system adapted to rural women is organised to support their income-generating activities.

The full enjoyment of the rights guaranteed by the Maputo Protocol is limited by various factors such as: – Women's ignorance of their rights and of the content of legal texts relating to human rights in general and women's rights in particular; – The non-integration of women as actors of dynamic and inclusive development, according to a rights-based approach; – The absence of optimal harmonisation of legislation with the provisions of the international conventions ratified; – The lack of specialisation of magistrates and the weakness of case law in matters of human rights in general and women's rights in particular; – The weak capacity of the institutions in charge of human rights; – The weak human and financial resources of human rights organisations in general and women's rights organisations in particular. – Difficulties in the implementation of certain rights due to the weight of sociological and cultural factors, the persistence of custom, and deeply rooted prejudices, in particular against women, which remain obstacles to the full realisation of women's rights according to the principles guaranteed by the Maputo Protocol.

Despite the Government's efforts to promote and protect women's rights, the Commission remains concerned about the following: i. The low representation of women in decision-making bodies; ii. Harmful socio-cultural constraints, the low involvement of women in political activities, and women's limited access to income and credit, to training and to information. i. The weakness of means of communication, which hinders, among other things, contact with displaced women and the recovery of women sex slaves and child soldiers held hostage by armed groups; ii.

Budgetary constraints that limit the care of rape survivors, iii. The presence of armed groups in certain regions of the country, iv. The difficulties in prosecuting members of armed groups who perpetrate sexual violence and in identifying them in cases of mass rape. i. The persistence of harmful practices inflicted on women, young women and girls, such as early marriage of girls (more than 51% of marriages in the DRC involve girls under 18), marriage by abduction, sexual violence and the maltreatment of widows; ii. The early sexuality of young girls, 45% of girls aged 16 to 18 have sexual relations with adults because of poverty, iii.

The prostitution of adolescents; iv. The use of rape, sexual mutilation and forced sterilisation as a weapon of war by armed groups. i. The criminalisation of any practice of abortion by Articles 166 and 167 of the Penal Code, which sentences persons who have performed an abortion to 5 to 15 years and the woman who undergoes the abortion to 5 to 10 years of imprisonment, although it has ratified the Maputo Protocol without reservations. ii. The absence of measures or legal instruments in favour of medical abortion, even in cases of sexual assault, rape or incest. i.

The persistence of socio-cultural constraints as well as the strong disparities between girls and boys at secondary level, and with regard to girls' and women's access to education and training. i. The major inequalities in the education sector, where there are fewer and fewer women in higher education compared to men, notably because of the sexual harassment to which girls are reportedly exposed; ii. Harassment in the workplace and in recruitment processes; iii. The harmful consequences of sexual harassment on women's access to education, training and the labour market. i.

The high level of domestic violence in Congolese society, whether physical, verbal or psychological; ii. Stereotypes and socio-cultural and religious constraints that contribute to women's internalisation of their supposed "inferiority", which justifies the various forms of violence against women; iii. The absence of a specific law punishing domestic violence. i. The absence of information on displaced and refugee women other than in the context of sexual violence, with no information on their care when they have not been victims of sexual violence. i.

The difficulties in implementing policies and programmes aimed at improving the conditions of older women, due to insufficient financial and material resources. i. The weakness of policies in favour of women with disabilities and the absence of a policy of assistance to families with children with disabilities. i. The feminisation and increase of HIV infection among young people
The State should continue to comply with its obligations under Article 26 of the Maputo Protocol and implement the recommendations of the Commission.
The State should take all measures for the domestication of the Maputo Protocol through the adoption of legislative texts and other administrative measures.
The State should continue its efforts to increase the representation of women in politics and in decision-making bodies, in application of the law on parity in politics.

The Commission recommends that the State: i. Strengthen the means of communication with a view to improving contact with displaced women and the recovery of women sex slaves and child soldiers held hostage by armed groups; ii. Increase the budget for the care of rape survivors, iii. Strengthen collaboration with MONUSCO in order to reinforce the security of the Congolese territory, iv. Pursue the efforts already undertaken concerning legal proceedings against members of armed groups who perpetrate sexual violence.

The Commission recommends that the State: i. Take the necessary measures to put an end to harmful practices towards women and girls such as early marriage, marriage by abduction, sexual violence and the maltreatment of widows; ii. Effectively combat the early sexuality and prostitution of young girls iii. Encourage the retention of girls in school; iv. Severely punish the use of rape, sexual mutilation and forced sterilisation as a weapon of war.
The State should: i. Take legislative measures with a view to decriminalising abortion. ii. Guarantee women access to medical abortion, in accordance with the provisions of the Maputo Protocol.

The State should take measures: i. To improve the enrolment rate of girls and prevent school dropout at secondary level, ii. Increase vocational training programmes for young girls; iii. Intensify awareness-raising on the importance of girls' schooling and their retention in school.

The Commission recommends that the State: i. Work towards reducing inequalities between men and women in the education sector, by effectively combating the sexual harassment to which girls are reportedly exposed; ii. Take measures to sanction harassment in the workplace, in recruitment processes, promotions and other social benefits, which are often conditional on the granting of sexual favours demanded of women by line managers or company heads; iii. Raise awareness of the harmful consequences of sexual harassment on women's access to education, training and the labour market; iv. Take support measures to help women who have been victims of harassment to reintegrate into working life.

The State should: i. Develop and adopt a specific law on domestic violence; ii. Conduct awareness-raising campaigns with a view to changing the behaviours that perpetuate domestic violence, in particular socio-cultural constraints, custom and tradition.

The State should: i. Take measures to strengthen the care of internally displaced, refugee, returnee and asylum-seeking women; ii. Put in place specific training and social reintegration programmes for displaced women and returnees iii. Put in place integration programmes for refugee and asylum-seeking women; iv. Find means of funding in order to adequately cover the needs of these different categories of women.
The State should take measures for the effective implementation of policies and programmes aimed at improving the conditions of older women.
The State should strengthen efforts for better care of women with disabilities and girls with disabilities in particular.

The State should: i. Take appropriate measures with a view to reducing women's vulnerability to HIV/AIDS; ii. Conduct information and awareness-raising campaigns for women concerning the different modes of transmission of and protection against HIV/AIDS.

The State should provide in the next periodic report all the information on the effective implementation of the recommendations made in these Concluding Observations. Adopted by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights at its 65th Ordinary Session, held from 21 October to 10 November 2019 in Banjul, Republic of The Gambia.
The State of Eritrea (Eritrea) is a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the African Charter), having ratified it on 14 January 1999.

Eritrea submitted its Initial and Combined Report to the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Commission) on 12 October 2017. The Report encompasses eight periodic reports, from the period between acceding to the African Charter in 1999 and 2016.
The Report was considered by the Commission during the 62 Ordinary Session, held in Nouakchott, Mauritania, from 25 April to 09 May 2018.

The Report was presented to the Commission by H.E. Mr. Tesfamicael Gerahtu, Ambassador and Head of the Delegation, in addition to the following members of the Delegation: - Mr. Adem Osman, First Secretary, Permanent Mission of the State of Eritrea to the United Nations (Geneva); - Mr. Biniam Berhe, First Secretary-Political Officer, Permanent Mission of the State of Eritrea to the African Union and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA); - Mr. Mussa Naib, Director General, Ministry of Education; - Mr. Sium Tecle, Staff, Legal Services, Ministry of Justice; - Mr. Mehretab Fessaie, Director General, Ministry of Labour and Human Welfare; - Dr. Mismay Ghebrewhiwet, Advisor to the Minister, Ministry of Health; AFRICAN UNION UNION AFRICAINE African Commission on Human & Peoples’ Rights UNIÃO AFRICANA Commission Africaine des Droits de l’Homme & des Peuples - Ms. Senait Lijam, Member, Executive Board, National Union of Eritrean Women; and - Mr. Ibrahim Abdu, Legal Services, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Commission:
Takes note of the effort made by Eritrea in preparing and presenting its overdue Initial periodic report, in accordance with the provisions of Article 62 of the African Charter;

Notes that Eritrea has ratified the following regional and international instruments on the promotion and protection of human rights: - The African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights; - The African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child; - The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; - The International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights; - The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women; - The Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment; - The Convention on the Rights of the Child; - The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict; - The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the sale of children, child prostitution and child pornography; - The International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination.
Welcomes the de-facto moratorium on the death penalty for the past ten years;

Commends the initiatives of the Eritrean Police Force, including introducing Community Policing with the aim of improving public safety, law and order, conducting a weekly regular radio program on civil order, public safety and crime prevention, and issuing a weekly newsletter on crime, prevention and public safety also appears in the official print media;

Notes the provision of education programs in prisons, including basic education up to secondary level, computer training and vocational programs in graphics and arts, as well as Arabic language programs which are offered on request;
Notes the establishment of an in-patient section at the National Referral Hospital in Asmara designated for referral of prisoners;
Notes the provision of HIV counselling centres in prison clinics;
Welcomes the opportunity given to Victims to participate in criminal proceedings, with the aim of obtaining redress for the Victims;
Welcomes the provision of legal services given to defendants who are hearing impaired;
Welcomes the establishment of the Immigration and Nationality Department to assist reintegration of Eritrean refugees;

Commends the provisions in the Citizenship Proclamation which stipulate that Eritrean citizenship can be acquired by birth, naturalization, adoption and marriage, which is equally applicable to men and women without discrimination;

Welcomes the laws, regulations and policies put in place to improve access to water, including the Eritrean Water Law 162/2010, the Potable Water Regulation 42/1998, Water Policy Paper of Eritrea and Eritrean Water Quality Standard;

Takes note of initiative of the Government to address malnutrition including establishing a Steering Committee on national food and nutrition security (FNSC), to improve access to safe, nutritious and affordable food;
Commends the establishment of 201 centres by the Government under the Hidri Programme, which sell subsidized food supplies to the public;

Welcomes the efforts by the Government to ensure social security and protection, including through enacting the National Pension Scheme (Proclamation 135/2003), the Public Sector Pension Scheme (Proclamation 136/2003) and the Marty’s’ Survivors Benefit Scheme (Proclamation 137/2003);
Notes that equal rights to employment are stipulated in the Labour Proclamation No. 118/2001, which also provides in Article 67 that employment may not be terminated during maternity leave;
Takes note of the Government’s initiatives to ensure access to free primary health, in accordance with the National Health Policy of 2010;
Commends the initiative on immunization through the Reach Every District Strategy for immunization, which is implemented in remote areas;

Takes notes of the Government’s program to eliminate maternal and neonatal tetanus, and the Roll Back Malaria Strategy which has resulted in reduction of malaria morbidity by 90% and a decrease by 86% of the overall mortality due to malaria;
Welcomes establishment of the HIV/AIDs Persons Association, which contributes to addressing stigmatization and marginalization of victims;
Welcomes the free provision of ARVs to 66% of the estimated eligible cases, by the Ministry of Health;
Commends the initiatives of the Government to end mother to child (MTCT) transmission, including integrating prevention services with antenatal care and providing HIV testing to pregnant women;

Commends the provision of free education in Eritrea at all levels, with limited expenses for transport and schools uniforms, and exemption for families from rural areas who cannot afford to pay for these expenses;
Takes note of the Government’s efforts to ensure equitable access to education, including improving access to schools for children who live in rural areas or come from nomadic communities;
Welcomes the programs initiated by the Government to combat adult illiteracy;
Commends the initiative of the Government to ensure preservation of cultural sites resulting in recognition of the capital city, Asmara, as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO on 08 July 2017;
Takes note of the Government initiatives aimed at reducing the maternal mortality ratio (MMR), with the annual rate of reduction MMR for the period 1990 to 2016 estimated at 4.6%;
Notes that the Transitional Civil Code protects the right to succession irrespective of gender or age;
Notes that Article 10(2) of Proclamation No. 86/1996 stipulates that 30% of the seats in the National Assemblies are reserved for women;
Welcomes the Eritrean Obstetric Fistula Repair Project, launched in 2002, to address and combat obstetric fistula;

Takes note of the National Policy on Children, in addition to the Working Group led by the Ministry of Labour and Human Welfare, which oversees implementation of the Convention of the Rights of the Child and the African Charter for the Rights and Welfare of the Child;
Notes that Article 607 of the Transitional Civil Code stipulates that the legal age of marriage is 18 years old, and that underage marriage is an offence and a ground for dissolution of the marriage;
Welcomes the criminalization of female genital mutilation (FGM) under Proclamation 148/2007, in addition to the establishment of 548 anti-FGM Committees nationwide;
Welcomes the reduction of FGM, noting that the practice which affected 89% of girls under the age of 5 in 1995, dropped to 5% by 2016;

Takes note of the National Policy on Persons with Disabilities, which ensures the implementation of equal rights and opportunities, which regulates the roles and responsibilities of all actors in advancing the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities,
Commends the loan scheme by the Ministry of Labour and Human Welfare which assists persons with disabilities start income-generating activities for gainful employment;
Appreciates the efforts to provide transportation for students with disabilities to attend school, such as the ‘Donkey for School’ project;
Commends provision of full medical care to 7,000 war-disabled persons with severe disabilities including their families.
Commends the ban on the use of plastic bags, through Legal Notice 63/2002, and the provision of local alternatives as a means to end plastic pollution;

Welcomes the conduction of environmental impact assessments prior to the commencement of any extractive activity. III. FACTORS RESTRICTING THE ENJOYMENT OF THE RIGHTS GUARANTEED IN THE AFRICAN CHARTER ON HUMAN AND PEOPLES’ RIGHTS

Eritrea was involved in a border dispute with its neighbour Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000. On 18 June 2000, the Governments of Eritrea and Ethiopia signed the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (CHA) and on 12 December 2000 the Algiers Peace Agreement was signed. However, the border dispute caused internal displacement of approximately 90,000 civilians, in addition to destruction of houses, places of worship and schools, among others. As a result, in addition to the destabilising effect of the conflict, nation building and provision and access to essential basic services, such as health facilities and schools, was hindered for a long time.

As a result of the hostilities with Ethiopia, civil and political rights and freedoms were severely restricted, including the rights to association and assembly, freedom of expression and information, movement, among others. Additionally, Presidential and legislative elections were indefinitely suspended, denying Eritrean citizens the right to to participate freely in the government and to freely chose representatives, in accordance with the provisions of the law. The Constitution was also suspended and the process of reviewing the constitution is incomplete.

Another factor restricting the enjoyment of human rights is the indefinite nature of the country’s National Service, which is an exception to forced labour under the Labour Proclamation and the definition of labour in the Penal Code. The practical effect of the indefinite extension of the period served in the National Service, is that conscripts can be required to serve for decades or, in some cases, indefinitely.
While recognising the efforts made by the Government to promote and protect human rights, the Commission is however concerned about the following:
No information has been provided on the domestication and incorporation of the African Charter, and other regional and international human rights instruments;
Eritrea is a State Party to only two regional human rights instruments;

The non-ratification of several relevant regional human rights instruments, including: - The OAU Convention Governing the Specific Aspects of Refugee Problems in Africa, 1974; - The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights (the Court Protocol), 2004; - The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa (the Maputo Protocol), 2005; - The African Union Convention on Preventing and Combating Corruption, 2006; - The African Youth Charter, 2009; - The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance, 2012; - The African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa (the Kampala Convention), 2012; - The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Older Persons in Africa; - The Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa;

The non-ratification of several relevant international human rights instruments, including: - The Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty, 1989; - The International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of their Families, 1990; - The Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, 2002; - The International Convention for the Protection of all Persons from Enforced Disappearance, 2006; - The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, 2006; and - The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, 2006; - The Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 2008;
The current laws do not stipulate the rights which cannot be limited under any circumstances, even in emergency situations;

The lack of: (i) Clarity on whether the Constitution (1997) is still in force and the delay in the finalization and adoption of the revised Constitution following the process which started in 2015; (ii) Mainstreaming of human rights in the domestic legal system, in addition to the fact there is no Ministry specifically designated to ensure that the promotion and protection of human rights is mainstreamed throughout the Government’s policies and programs; (iii) An independent national institution entrusted with the promotion and protection of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the African Charter; (iv) A recent census on the population in the country, which would guide the formulation of policies and programs on the protection of human rights in the country;
The death penalty is retained in the Transitional Penal Code of Eritrea;
The lack of specific legislation criminalizing extra-judicial killings;
The situation of deaths in the prisons or other places of detentions;
The reported deaths of members of the Jehovah Witness faith in detention;

It is noted in the Report that torture is not condoned in the domestic laws and is punishable by law, however no information is provided on the exact legal provisions which prohibit torture, or the existence of a law defining and criminalizing torture;
No information is provided of statistics on the number of cases of torture reported, investigated and prosecuted;
There is no independent institution mandated to conduct investigations on allegations of torture;
The absence of information on independent investigations on the reports of torture committed on persons in detention;

The absence of information in the Report on the following: (i) The total number of prisons and other centres of detention in the country; (ii) The total prison population in the country, in addition to the number of remand prisoners verses convicted persons, female and male prisoners, in addition to juvenile prisoners; (iii) The number of prisoners currently sentenced to capital punishment, in light of the information provided that the “death penalty is exceptionally applied for criminal offences that entail capital punishment;” (iv) The number of meals each prisoners receives daily, and whether the meals meet international standards; (v) The percentage of the prison population with HIV/AIDS, and whether these prisoners have free access to ARVs; (vi) The total number of prison officials, in addition to the number of female officers; (vii) Training specifically related to human rights provided to law enforcement agencies, including the Eritrean Police Force, the Eritrea Correctional and Rehabilitation Services and the Community Police, in addition to whether the Prison Services Regulation contains provisions on human rights and the rights of detained persons; (viii) Whether Government has a condom distribution program in prisons, as a way to curb the HIV/AIDS epidemic; (ix) The Ministry responsible for overseeing the Eritrea Correctional and Rehabilitation Services;
There is no independent institution mandated to conduct unannounced visits to prisons and other places of detention;
Lack of access by family members to prisoners held in incommunicado detention.

The continued denial of the basic rights of all persons detained without access to lawyers or a fair and speedy trial, including specifically the group of former Government officials, journalists and the Jehovah Witness religious leaders, who were arrested, never charged or tried in a court of law, or allowed access to lawyers or their families;
The lack of legal provisions stipulating the right of habeas corpus;
The lack of legislation or policy which ensures access to legal aid;
The lack of clarity on the position of the Special Court within the hierarchy of the judicial system;

Certain provisions in the Proclamation No.85/1996, which established the Special Court, which are contrary to the right to a fair trial including: Article 4(2) which states that “the Special Court can review and see again previously decided cases,” in violation of the principle of res judicata; Articles 3 and 6 which provide that the “the Special Court may disregard the provisions of the Penal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code of Eritrea;” and Article 5(1) which denies the right of appeal of a Special Court decision;
Insufficient information on the process of appointing judges, in addition to legal provisions stipulating their independence and security of tenure;
The lack of information on whether the judges of the Community Courts, the Military Courts and the Special Court are required to have prior training and legal experience;
The lack of information on an institution which conducts regular training for judicial officers, including training on human rights issues;
The lack of clarity on the Ministry which monitors implementation of Proclamation 73/1995, which details “the operation of new faiths, with funding from external sources;”
The lack of provisions in the Proclamation provide for recourse to appeal to the Courts for religious groups whose applications for registration are denied;
The forfeiture of citizenship rights of followers of Jehovah Witness faith, in response to their refusal to vote in the 1993 independence referendum, exposing them to de facto statelessness;
The lack of clarity on the existence of a law which expressly provides for the right to access information;
The restriction on freedom of expression in the Penal Code which criminalizes defamation;
There is no private media in the country in accordance with the Press Proclamation 90/1996 which stipulates that ownership of television and radio is reserved for the Government;
There is no independent regulatory body which exercises powers in the areas of broadcast or telecommunications regulation;
The restricted access to telephone SIM cards;
The heavy restriction of the Internet, with limited access to the Internet throughout the country;

The lack of information on the existence and total number of independent civil society organizations (CSOs) operating in the country, distinguished from the ‘national organizations’ mentioned in the Report;

Insufficient information on the process of registration for non-governmental organizations under Legal Notice No 5 of 1992, including whether there is recourse to appeal for organizations whose application is denied;
The lack of information on the criteria and requirements for holding a peaceful assembly;
Absence of information on a national policy to reduce migration and encourage the return of Eritrean diaspora;
Severe restrictions on movement of citizens, in particular conscripted youth whose freedom of movement inside and out of the country is heavily curtailed, contrary to Article 12(1) of the Charter;
The requirement for an exit visa for Eritreans who wish to leave the country, with children under the age of five (5) not eligible to be issued an exit visa;
The lack of an appeal process for persons denied the exit visa;
